summary: Zhuan Dao was a Buddhist studies scholar who studied under Tongzhi. He founded Poh Tho Si in 1911 and Kong Meng San Phor Kark See Monastery in 1920.
Zijie Li is a Buddhist studies scholar who studied at Komazawa University and held a post at the Japan Society for the Promotion of Science as a 特別研究員DC (both attested 2015).

Zoltán Gombocz (1877–1935) worked in linguistics and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Berzsenyi Dániel Evangélikus Gimnázium until 1895 and at Eötvös Loránd University from 1895 to 1900.

Zong Rinpoche (1905–1984) was a Tibetology and Buddhist studies scholar who studied under Trijang Rinpoche and Dechen Nyingpo at Ganden Shartse Monastery and Gyuto Monastery. He served as Abbot of Ganden Shartse (1937–1946) and Rektor of the Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies (1967–1971).

Zsóka Gelle works in Tibetology and Buddhist studies. She studied at Berzsenyi Dániel Teacher Training College, Eötvös Loránd University, Manjushree Centre of Tibetan Culture, and University of Vienna, and held posts including lecturer at Dharma Gate Buddhist College and Khyentse Fellow (2014–2016).

Zuicho Tachibana (1890–1968) was an Iranian and Central Asian studies, Buddhist studies, and history and archaeology scholar. He studied under Kozui Otani from around 1903 to 1914 and under Edward Denison Ross from around 1910 to 1912.

Zuiei Ito (1942–2020) was a Buddhist studies and Indology scholar educated at Waseda University and the University of Tokyo. He served as professor of Buddhist studies at Rissho University (1980–2013) and held lecturer posts at Waseda, Shinshu, and Tokyo universities.

Zuigan Goto (1879–1965) was a Buddhist and religious studies scholar. He studied at the Second Higher School, the University of Tokyo (1903–1906), and under Sokatsu Shaku (~1900–1914), later serving as president of Hanazono University in 1932.

Zuiho Yamaguchi (1926–2023) was a Tibetologist and Buddhist studies scholar who studied at the University of Tokyo, École Pratique des Hautes Études, and under Jacques Bacot and Rolf Alfred Stein. He held posts at Toyo Bunko, CNRS, the University of Tokyo, and Nagoya University.

Zuiryu Nakamura (1915–1995) worked in Buddhist studies and Tibetology. He studied under Kenryu Tsukinowa and Susumu Yamaguchi, became a professor at Rissho University in 1945, and served as director of the Institute for the Comprehensive Study of Lotus Sutra.
Zur Mang Khenpo Pema Namgyal studied under Shenphen Nangwa and Pema Wangchok Gyelpo.
pad+ma la studied under Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche and Dudjom Rinpoche.

Édouard Chavannes (1865–1918) was a sinologist, Buddhist scholar, and Central Asian specialist educated at École Normale Supérieure, Collège de France, and INALCO under Marie-Jean-Léon d'Hervey de Saint Denys. He was a professor at Collège de France (1893–1918).

Édouard Huber (1879–1914) was a sinologist, indologist, and Buddhist studies scholar who studied at the Sorbonne, University of Paris, and Collège de France under Sylvain Lévi and Johann Baptist Schibenegg. He was a director at EFEO from 1901 to 1905.

Émile Benveniste (1902–1976) was a linguist, indologist, and Iranian specialist educated at the University of Paris and EPHE under Antoine Meillet, Sylvain Lévi, and others. He served as directeur d’études at EPHE (1927–1969) and chair at Collège de France (1937–1969).
Émile Chartier (1868–1951) was a philosopher who studied at Lycée Pierre-Corneille from around 1886 to 1889 and École Normale Supérieure from around 1889 to 1892.

Émile Chatelain (1851–1933) was a scholar of history, archaeology, and linguistics who studied at the École Pratique des Hautes Études (1872–1876). He held posts at the École française de Rome (1876–1877) and the École Pratique des Hautes Études (~1877–1925).

Émile Durkheim (1858–1917) was a sociologist and religious studies scholar educated at École Normale Supérieure and under Wilhelm Wundt in Leipzig. He held professorships at the University of Bordeaux (1887–1902) and Sorbonne University (around 1902–1917).

Émile Senart (1847–1928) was an Indology and Buddhist studies scholar who studied at Munich and Göttingen under Theodor Benfey. He held a professorship at the Collège de France and served as president of the Société Asiatique from 1908 to 1928.

Émile-Louis Burnouf (1821–1907) was an indologist and linguist who studied at the École Normale Supérieure, University of Paris, and with Eugène Burnouf. He was a professor at the University of Nancy (1854–1867) and director of the École française d'Athènes (1867–1875).
